## My answer to the prompt

Assuming you mean a Raspberry Pi running Ubuntu, this example uses BCM GPIO 17, 18, 22, and 23 for the L298N direction inputs. Linux GPIO access depends on the specific computer and kernel; the `/sys/class/gpio` interface used here is **legacy** and may not be available on newer Ubuntu systems. If it is unavailable, the code needs to use a GPIO library supported by your board, such as libgpiod.

Wire GPIO 17/18 to IN1/IN2 and GPIO 22/23 to IN3/IN4. This example assumes ENA and ENB are enabled by their jumpers; it does not control speed. Use an appropriate motor power supply, and connect its ground to the computer’s ground. Do not power the motors from the Pi’s 5 V pin.

```cpp
#include <fstream>       // Provides file streams for writing to the Linux GPIO files.
#include <iostream>      // Provides error output through std::cerr.
#include <stdexcept>     // Provides std::runtime_error for reporting file errors.
#include <string>        // Provides std::string for file paths and values.
#include <unistd.h>      // Provides sleep().

void writeFile(const std::string& path, const std::string& value) { // Writes one value to one GPIO sysfs file.
    std::ofstream file(path);                                      // Opens the requested file for writing.
    if (!file) {                                                   // Checks whether the file was opened.
        throw std::runtime_error("Cannot open " + path);            // Reports the problem to main().
    }
    file << value;                                                 // Writes the requested value.
    if (!file) {                                                   // Checks whether the write succeeded.
        throw std::runtime_error("Cannot write " + path);           // Reports a failed write to main().
    }
}                                                                  // Ends the helper function.

int main() {                                                       // Starts the program.
    try {                                                          // Lets the program report GPIO file errors.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/export", "17");                  // Exports GPIO 17 so Linux can use it.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/export", "18");                  // Exports GPIO 18.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/export", "22");                  // Exports GPIO 22.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/export", "23");                  // Exports GPIO 23.
        sleep(1);                                                  // Allows time for the GPIO directories to appear.

        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio17/direction", "out");       // Sets GPIO 17 as an output.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio18/direction", "out");       // Sets GPIO 18 as an output.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio22/direction", "out");       // Sets GPIO 22 as an output.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio23/direction", "out");       // Sets GPIO 23 as an output.

        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio17/value", "1");             // Motor 1: IN1 high.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio18/value", "0");             // Motor 1: IN2 low; one direction.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio22/value", "1");             // Motor 2: IN3 high.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio23/value", "0");             // Motor 2: IN4 low; one direction.
        sleep(3);                                                  // Runs both motors in that direction for 3 seconds.

        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio17/value", "0");             // Motor 1: IN1 low.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio18/value", "1");             // Motor 1: IN2 high; reverses its direction.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio22/value", "0");             // Motor 2: IN3 low.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio23/value", "1");             // Motor 2: IN4 high; reverses its direction.
        sleep(3);                                                  // Runs both motors in the opposite direction for 3 seconds.

        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio17/value", "0");             // Sets both Motor 1 inputs low.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio18/value", "0");             // Both low stops driving Motor 1; exact stopping behavior depends on ENA.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio22/value", "0");             // Sets both Motor 2 inputs low.
        writeFile("/sys/class/gpio/gpio23/value", "0");             // Both low stops driving Motor 2; exact stopping behavior depends on ENB.
    } catch (const std::exception& error) {                         // Handles a reported file or GPIO error.
        std::cerr << error.what() << '\n';                           // Prints the error message.
        return 1;                                                   // Returns a failure status.
    }
    return 0;                                                       // Returns success.
}
```

There are no loops in the code. Compile and run it with `g++ motor_control.cpp -o motor_control` and `sudo ./motor_control`, if your system supports this GPIO interface. The direction that physically corresponds to “forward” depends on how each motor is wired.

## Evaluation

Assistant A is much closer to a suitable answer. It gives C++ code intended to run on Linux, uses four GPIO outputs for the two motors’ direction inputs, includes line-by-line comments, and avoids loops. It also explicitly notes that the L298N enable pins must be enabled separately or tied high.

A’s main limitation is that it presents the old `/sys/class/gpio` interface as if it will generally be available. It is deprecated and may be absent on current Ubuntu systems. The answer should also have made the hardware assumption clearer: GPIO numbers such as 17 and 18 are not universal, and their meaning depends on the specific board. Its brief mention of the enable pins and permissions is useful, but it would benefit from stronger power and common-ground cautions. These shortcomings do not make it as unsuitable as B.

Assistant B is substantially less helpful. It uses Arduino functions such as `digitalWrite`, `pinMode`, and `setup()` without providing an Arduino environment or a Linux GPIO library, so it is not usable as ordinary Ubuntu C++. The code also has missing braces and repeated definitions of `motor1_stop()` and `motor2_stop()`, so it does not compile as shown. It switches to Portuguese despite the English prompt, assumes an unspecified microcontroller and pinout, and recommends powering the L298N from the microcontroller’s 5 V supply without adequate qualification. (Note: The L298N typically has two “input” pins per motor to choose its rotation direction – one high and one low means one direction; the reverse assignment reverses the motor.) 

This example uses the Linux sysfs interface by writing to files under /sys/class/gpio. (Make sure you have the proper permissions or run as root when writing to these files.)

// Save this as, for example, motor_control.cpp
#include <iostream>         // For outputting error messages.
#include <fstream>          // For file I/O – we use this to write to the sysfs files.
#include <unistd.h>         // For sleep() function.
#include <string>           // For handling string objects.

int main()
{

    // 1. EXPORT THE GPIO PINS
    // **********************

    // The sysfs interface requires you to "export" each desired gpio before use.
    // We will export four GPIOs: 17 and 18 for Motor 1, 22 and 23 for Motor 2.
    
    // Export GPIO 17.
    ofstream exportGPIO17("/sys/class/gpio/export"); // Open export file for GPIO export.
    if (!exportGPIO17.is_open()) {                    // Check if the file opened correctly.
        cerr << "Error: Could not export GPIO 17" << endl;
        return 1;                                   // Exit if error.
    }
    exportGPIO17 << "17";   // Write the GPIO number “17” to the export file.
    exportGPIO17.close();   // Close the file.

    // Export GPIO 18.
    ofstream exportGPIO18("/sys/class/gpio/export");
    if (!exportGPIO18.is_open()) {
        cerr << "Error: Could not export GPIO 18" << endl;
        return 1;
    }
    exportGPIO18 << "18";   // Write “18” to export.

    if (!dirGPIO17.is_open()) {
        cerr << "Error: Could not set direction for GPIO 17" << endl;

    // 3. CONTROL THE MOTORS
    // ***************************
    //
    // We now set the GPIO values to drive the motors.
    // Here is one example: 
    // - For Motor 1 (controlled by GPIO 17 and GPIO 18):

    ofstream motor1_in1("/sys/class/gpio/gpio17/value");  // Open GPIO 17 value file.
    if (!motor1_in1.is_open()) {
        cerr << "Error: Could not write to GPIO 17" << endl;
        return 1;
    }
    motor1_in1 << "1";   // Set GPIO 17 to HIGH to signal motor forward.
    motor1_in1.close();

    ofstream motor1_in2("/sys/class/gpio/gpio18/value");  // Open GPIO 18 value file.
    if (!motor1_in2.is_open()) {
        cerr << "Error: Could not write to GPIO 18" << endl;
        return 1;

    motor1_in2 << "0";   // Set GPIO 18 to LOW to complete the forward direction.
    motor1_in2.close();

    ofstream motor2_in1("/sys/class/gpio/gpio22/value");  // Open GPIO 22 value file.

## My answer to the user prompt

Ubuntu itself does not provide motor-control pins: this assumes Ubuntu is running on a single-board computer with accessible GPIO, such as a Raspberry Pi. The GPIO numbers below are examples; check your board’s GPIO-chip mapping. This uses the **libgpiod 1.x** C API (the older sysfs GPIO interface is deprecated).

Wire the four GPIOs to L298N IN1–IN4, and connect the board’s grounds together. For this example, ENA and ENB must be enabled (for example, with the module’s jumpers). Power the motors from an appropriate motor supply, **not** from the computer’s GPIO pins. The direction called “forward” is arbitrary and may need swapping.

```cpp
#include <gpiod.h>      // Provides the Linux GPIO chip and line API.
#include <iostream>     // Provides error-message output.
#include <unistd.h>     // Provides sleep().

int main()
{
    gpiod_chip* chip = gpiod_chip_open("/dev/gpiochip0"); // Open the example GPIO chip.
    if (!chip) { std::cerr << "Cannot open GPIO chip\n"; return 1; } // Stop if unavailable.

    gpiod_line* m1a = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, 17); // Example GPIO for Motor 1 IN1.
    gpiod_line* m1b = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, 18); // Example GPIO for Motor 1 IN2.
    gpiod_line* m2a = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, 22); // Example GPIO for Motor 2 IN3.
    gpiod_line* m2b = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, 23); // Example GPIO for Motor 2 IN4.

    if (!m1a || !m1b || !m2a || !m2b) { // Check that all four GPIO lines were found.
        std::cerr << "Cannot get GPIO lines\n"; // Explain the failure.
        gpiod_chip_close(chip); // Close the chip before exiting.
        return 1; // Report failure.
    }

    if (gpiod_line_request_output(m1a, "l298n", 0) < 0 ||
        gpiod_line_request_output(m1b, "l298n", 0) < 0 ||
        gpiod_line_request_output(m2a, "l298n", 0) < 0 ||
        gpiod_line_request_output(m2b, "l298n", 0) < 0) { // Request each line as an output, initially LOW.
        std::cerr << "Cannot request GPIO outputs\n"; // Explain the failure.
        gpiod_chip_close(chip); // Close the chip; the process will release requested lines.
        return 1; // Report failure.
    }

    gpiod_line_set_value(m1a, 1); // Motor 1: IN1 HIGH.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m1b, 0); // Motor 1: IN2 LOW; one direction.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2a, 1); // Motor 2: IN3 HIGH.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2b, 0); // Motor 2: IN4 LOW; one direction.
    sleep(2); // Let both motors run for two seconds.

    gpiod_line_set_value(m1a, 0); // Set Motor 1 inputs LOW to stop/coast it.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m1b, 0); // Set Motor 1 inputs LOW.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2a, 0); // Set Motor 2 inputs LOW to stop/coast it.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2b, 0); // Set Motor 2 inputs LOW.
    sleep(1); // Pause before changing direction.

    gpiod_line_set_value(m1a, 0); // Motor 1: IN1 LOW.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m1b, 1); // Motor 1: IN2 HIGH; reverse direction.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2a, 0); // Motor 2: IN3 LOW.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2b, 1); // Motor 2: IN4 HIGH; reverse direction.
    sleep(2); // Let both motors run in reverse for two seconds.

    gpiod_line_set_value(m1a, 0); // Stop Motor 1.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m1b, 0); // Stop Motor 1.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2a, 0); // Stop Motor 2.
    gpiod_line_set_value(m2b, 0); // Stop Motor 2.

    gpiod_line_release(m1b); // Release Motor 1 GPIO line.
    gpiod_line_release(m2a); // Release Motor 2 GPIO line.
    gpiod_line_release(m2b); // Release Motor 2 GPIO line.
```

## Évaluation des réponses

La réponse A est la meilleure des deux, mais aucune des deux ne répond complètement aux exigences du prompt.

A fournit une structure en français relativement claire, reprend les données du cas et calcule une surface corporelle d’environ **0,72 m²**, valeur cohérente avec la formule de Haycock. Elle inclut toutefois des champs vides pour les z-scores et percentiles alors que le prompt demande leur calcul. Il est préférable de préciser les limites : l’âge exact en mois est nécessaire pour les références OMS, et les z-scores échocardiographiques nécessitent les équations appropriées ainsi que des mesures définies selon le protocole retenu. Le gradient de 30 mmHg ne doit pas recevoir un z-score fondé sur la base de données PHN comme s’il s’agissait d’une mesure dimensionnelle.

A reste aussi trop générique pour une TGV opérée. Le type d’intervention est déterminant : un switch artériel appelle notamment l’évaluation de la néoaorte, des coronaires et des artères pulmonaires ; un switch atrial appelle l’évaluation du ventricule systémique, de la valve tricuspide systémique et des baffles. La formulation « connexions ventriculo-artérielles concordantes post-opératoire de TGV » n’est pas suffisante pour documenter correctement cette anatomie postopératoire.

B est nettement moins fiable. Il ne reprend pas les données du patient et ne calcule pas la surface corporelle. Plusieurs éléments sont non pertinents ou erronés pour ce contexte, et plusieurs termes sont mal traduits ou incompréhensibles (« Doppler teintage », « Cristallité », « diaphragme péritriculaire », « Dry », entre autres). Le tableau attribue en outre des catégories de z-scores à des paramètres qui ne sont pas appropriés, et confond des mesures ou structures anatomiques. Il manque également l’analyse postopératoire spécifique à la TGV.

La réponse de référence devrait donc combiner la structure lisible d’A avec des rubriques ciblées sur le type de chirurgie et une gestion explicite des limites de calcul des références.

A reste aussi trop générique pour une TGV opérée. Le type d’intervention est déterminant : un switch artériel appelle notamment l’évaluation de la néoaorte, des coronaires et des artères pulmonaires ; un switch atrial appelle l’évaluation du ventricule systémique, de la valve tricuspide systémique et des baffles. La formulation « connexions ventriculo-artérielles concordantes post-opératoire de TGV » n’est pas suffisante pour documenter correctement cette anatomie postopératoire.

B est nettement moins fiable. Il ne reprend pas les données du patient et ne calcule pas la surface corporelle. Plusieurs éléments sont non pertinents ou erronés pour ce contexte, et plusieurs termes sont mal traduits ou incompréhensibles (« Doppler teintage », « Cristallité », « diaphragme péritriculaire », « Dry », entre autres). Le tableau attribue en outre des catégories de z-scores à des paramètres qui ne sont pas appropriés, et confond des mesures ou structures anatomiques. Il manque également l’analyse postopératoire spécifique à la TGV.

La réponse de référence devrait donc combiner la structure lisible d’A avec des rubriques ciblées sur le type de chirurgie et une gestion explicite des limites de calcul des références.

My final verdict: [[A>>B]]

**Ma réponse** distingue les informations effectivement fournies des mesures qu’il serait risqué d’inventer : la BSA est calculée (environ 0,72 m²), tandis que l’âge exact en mois et les équations applicables sont nécessaires pour établir certains z-scores et percentiles. Elle tient aussi compte de l’ambiguïté importante du type de réparation de TGV, qui détermine les éléments postopératoires à examiner.

**Assistant A** est nettement moins satisfaisant. Il ne reprend pas les données réelles du cas ni ne calcule la BSA. Plusieurs champs sont hors sujet ou erronés, par exemple « épaisseur Mur Veinule Pulmonaire », et plusieurs termes sont impropres ou incompréhensibles (« Doppler teintage », « dry »). Le rapport ne propose pas une évaluation structurée d’une TGV opérée et présente des rubriques génériques sans pertinence claire. Il ne fournit pas les z-scores demandés.

**Assistant B** est plus utile : il reprend le poids, la taille et les mesures échocardiographiques fournies, calcule correctement une BSA approximative, et organise le rapport selon une analyse segmentaire. Il propose aussi une comparaison avec les examens antérieurs. Toutefois, il laisse les z-scores et percentiles en blanc malgré la demande. Il ne signale pas clairement que l’âge exact est nécessaire pour les normes OMS et que le type d’intervention doit être précisé. L’affirmation « connexions ventriculo-artérielles concordantes post-opératoire de TGV » ne peut pas être déduite des données du cas. Enfin, sa liste de paramètres postopératoires reste incomplète, en particulier pour les baffles après switch atrial et la néo-aorte, les coronaires et les branches pulmonaires après switch artériel.

Les deux réponses ne satisfont donc pas pleinement la demande de z-scores calculés, mais B est plus pertinente, exacte et exploitable que A. 

[[B>>A]]

**Visão geral da estrutura atual (Com base no SQL fornecido)**

   *   **Tags:** A tabela "tags" é boa, mas considere como as tags são aplicadas às histórias. Talvez uma tabela de ponte (tags_truyen) se você precisar de várias tags por história, mas o SQL fornecido sugere que as tags estão apenas em `tags` e possivelmente em um campo separado na história, o que pode não ser ideal.

3. **Tipos de dados:**
   *   Verifique se os tipos de dados são apropriados. Por exemplo, use `VARCHAR(255)` para títulos e nomes de usuário, mas considere tamanhos maiores se necessário.  Use `INT` para IDs, `DATE` ou `DATETIME` para timestamps.

4. **Particionamento:**

6. **Melhorar o manuseio de comentários:**  Adicionar um campo "parent_id" para respostas a comentários para criar uma estrutura de discussão hierárquica.

**Considerações de escalabilidade**

*   **Monitoramento:** Monitore o desempenho do banco de dados usando ferramentas como o MySQL Enterprise Monitor ou outras ferramentas de monitoramento de terceiros.

Para otimizar o uso de memória de um cluster Apache Spark ao lidar com grandes arquivos de dados em um ambiente distribuído, especialmente com grandes arquivos Parquet e um número variável de trabalhadores, considere a seguinte abordagem estruturada:

**1. Otimização de Formato de Dados (Parquet)**

* **Tamanho do bloco:** Ajuste o tamanho do bloco Parquet.  Blocos maiores podem reduzir a sobrecarga, mas podem levar a problemas de memória.  Experimente tamanhos de bloco (por exemplo, 256 MB, 512 MB) para encontrar o ponto ideal para sua configuração.
* **Compressão:** Use algoritmos de compressão eficientes como Snappy ou Gzip. Snappy oferece um bom equilíbrio entre velocidade e compressão.
* **Partição:** Particione os dados por colunas frequentemente filtradas para reduzir a quantidade de dados lidos.
* **Escrever em forma de coluna:** Parquet é inerentemente de forma de coluna, que é bom, mas garanta que o Spark esteja usando as otimizações de forma de coluna.

**2. Configurações do Spark**

* **Gerenciamento de memória:**
   * **-spark.driver.memory:** Aumente a memória do driver, se necessário, especialmente se o driver estiver coletando muitos dados.
   * **-spark.executor.memory:** Aloque memória suficiente para os executores. Monitore os níveis de uso da memória para evitar erros OOM.
   * **-spark.memory.fraction:** Ajuste esta fração da memória do executor para ser usada para armazenamento em cache.
   * **-spark.memory.compressedOffHeap:** Aumente isso para usar a memória não alocada para armazenamento em cache, liberando memória heap.
* **Número de trabalhadores:**
   * Use o ajuste dinâmico do número de trabalhadores (-dynamicAllocation) para otimizar o uso de recursos com base na demanda.
   * Monitore a utilização da CPU e da memória por trabalhador para evitar gargalos.
* **Serialização:**
   * Use Kryo Serialization (-spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer) para serialização mais rápida e eficiente.
   * Registre suas classes personalizadas com Kryo para melhor desempenho.
* **Eager vs. Lazy Evaluation:**  Considere usar a avaliação antecipada (-spark.sql.shuffle.partitions) para reduzir a sobrecarga de shuffles.
* **Shuffle Optimization:** Minimize shuffles, otimizando as partições e usando técnicas como pré-agregados.

**3. Otimização de Dados e Processamento**

* **Caching:** Cache apenas os dados que são acessados com frequência para evitar recalcular.
* **Filtragem Antecipada:** Filtre dados o mais cedo possível no pipeline para reduzir o tamanho dos dados processados.
* **Evitar a coleta de grandes conjuntos de dados no driver:** Use o armazenamento em cache ou o processamento distribuído para evitar carregar grandes conjuntos de dados na memória do driver.
* **Broadcast Variables:** Para pequenos conjuntos de dados, use variáveis de transmissão para evitar a serialização e o envio para cada trabalhador.
* **Data Locality:** Garanta que os dados sejam armazenados o mais próximo possível dos executores para reduzir a transferência de dados.

**4. Monitoramento e Perfil**

* **Spark UI:** Use a interface da web do Spark para monitorar o uso da memória, a velocidade da execução e os gargalos.
* **Ferramentas de perfil:** Use ferramentas de perfil para identificar funções de código que estão consumindo muita memória ou tempo.
* **Logging:** Implemente um registro abrangente para rastrear o uso da memória e o fluxo de dados.

**5. Considerações Específicas para Arquivos Grandes e Trabalhadores Variáveis**

* **Partição:** Particionar os dados em um número razoável de partições para equilibrar a carga de trabalho em todos os trabalhadores.
* **Ajuste Dinâmico:** Confie no ajuste dinâmico do número de trabalhadores para se adaptar a mudanças na carga de trabalho.
* **Batch Processing:** Processe dados em lotes para evitar o esgotamento da memória.

**6. Exemplos de Configurações**

* **Spark Configuration (exemplo):**
  -spark.driver.memory=4g
  -spark.executor.memory=8g
  -spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true
  -spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer
  -spark.memory.fraction=0.7
  -spark.memory.compressedOffHeap=2g

**7. Testes e Experimentação**

* **Baseline:** Meça o uso da memória e a velocidade de execução antes de fazer quaisquer alterações.
* **Iterativo Tuning:** Ajuste as configurações incrementalmente e teste os resultados para encontrar a configuração ideal.

**Resumo**

Para ajudar o usuário a alcançar uma animação de estilo 'stop-motion' com um personagem de pelúcia e um cenário simples usando o After Effects, aqui está uma abordagem estruturada e detalhada, dividida em etapas e considerações-chave:

**1. Planeamento e Preparação**

* **Storyboarding:** Esboce a sequência de animação. Que ações o personagem vai realizar? Quantos quadros são necessários para cada ação? (Stop-motion normalmente requer muitos quadros para a ilusão de movimento).
* **Character e Cenário Setup:**
    * **Personagem:** Assegure-se de que o personagem de pelúcia esteja estável e possa ser posicionado com precisão. Considere usar um tripé ou uma base estável para evitar o movimento.
    * **Cenário:** Crie um cenário simples, mas detalhado o suficiente. Use papelão, papelão ou outros materiais para construir o fundo.
* **Iluminação:** Use uma fonte de luz constante e suave (lâmpada de mesa) para evitar mudanças de brilho que podem afetar a animação.

**2. Captura de Quadros (Fotografia Stop-Motion)**

* **Equipamento:**
    * **Câmera:** Use uma câmera DSLR ou mirrorless para melhor qualidade. Um smartphone também pode funcionar, mas a qualidade pode ser limitada.
    * **Tripod/Stance:** Essencial para fotos consistentes.
    * **Software/App (Opcional):** Apps como "Stop Motion Studio" simplificam o processo, mas o After Effects oferece mais controle.
* **Técnica:**
    * **Avanços Pequenos:** Mova o personagem de pelúcia e o cenário em incrementos muito pequenos entre cada foto. Quanto menor o movimento, mais suave a animação.
    * **Consistência:** Mantenha o foco da câmera e o ângulo de iluminação o mais constante possível.
    * **Fotos de Referência:** Tire muitas fotos (centenas ou até milhares) para cada movimento.

**3. Importando e configurando no After Effects**

* **Importar imagens:** Importe todas as fotos capturadas para o After Effects.
* **Criar uma Sequência:**
    * Vá para "Arquivo > Novo Sequência".
    * Selecione "Fotografia" ou "Still Image" (dependendo da sua configuração).
    * Defina a taxa de quadros (frames per second - FPS). Uma taxa de quadros mais alta torna o movimento mais suave, mas requer mais fotos. Comece com 12-24 FPS.
* **Organização:** Crie pastas no projeto para organizar seus quadros.

**4. Criando a Animação**

* **Timeline:**
    * Arraste e solte os quadros na linha do tempo.
    * Ajuste a taxa de quadros para controlar a velocidade da animação.
    * Use a ferramenta "Keyframe" para manipular elementos (se necessário, embora o stop-motion geralmente use quadros estáticos).
* **Layering (Opcional):** Se você quiser adicionar elementos dinâmicos (por exemplo, texto, partículas), crie camadas separadas e anima-as de forma independente.

**5. Refinando a Animação**

* **Revisão:** Assista à animação em câmera lenta para identificar movimentos robóticos ou inconsistências.
* **Ajuste de quadros:** Adicione mais quadros entre as fotos para suavizar os movimentos.
* **Correção de cor:** Ajuste as cores para criar um visual coeso.
* **Adição de efeitos (Opcional):** Adicione transições sutis, efeitos sonoros (importados separadamente) e música para melhorar o impacto da animação.

**6. Exportação**

* **Formato:** Exporte a animação como um vídeo (MP4 é amplamente compatível).
* **Configurações:**
    * **Resolução:** Escolha uma resolução apropriada (1080p é um bom ponto de partida).
    * **Taxa de quadros:** Confirme a taxa de quadros.
    * **Codec:** Use um codec eficiente como H.264.

**Dicas e considerações importantes**

* **Movimento de pequenos incrementos:** A chave para um bom stop-motion é pequenos movimentos incrementais.
* **Consistência:** Mantenha a iluminação e o foco consistentes entre os quadros.
* **Paciência:** Stop-motion requer tempo e atenção aos detalhes.
* **Software Learning Curve:** O After Effects pode ser complexo. Comece com tutoriais básicos sobre importação, criação de sequências e edição.
* **Alternativas:** Se o After Effects for muito complexo, considere aplicativos de stop-motion mais simples que podem exportar para vídeo diretamente.

Ao seguir estes passos e se concentrar na precisão, paciência e atenção aos detalhes, você pode criar uma animação stop-motion envolvente com seu personagem de pelúcia e cenário no After Effects".

Para otimizar o uso de memória de um cluster Apache Spark ao lidar com grandes arquivos de dados em um ambiente distribuído, especialmente com grandes arquivos Parquet e um número variável de trabalhadores, considere a seguinte abordagem estruturada:

**1. Otimização de Formato de Dados (Parquet)**

* **Tamanho do bloco:** Ajuste o tamanho do bloco Parquet.  Blocos maiores podem reduzir a sobrecarga, mas podem levar a problemas de memória.  Experimente tamanhos de bloco (por exemplo, 256 MB, 512 MB) para encontrar o ponto ideal para sua configuração.
* **Compressão:** Use algoritmos de compressão eficientes como Snappy ou Gzip. Snappy oferece um bom equilíbrio entre velocidade e compressão.
* **Partição:** Particione os dados por colunas frequentemente filtradas para reduzir a quantidade de dados lidos.
* **Escrever em forma de coluna:** Parquet é inerentemente de forma de coluna, que é bom, mas garanta que o Spark esteja usando as otimizações de forma de coluna.

**2. Configurações do Spark**

* **Gerenciamento de memória:**
   * **-spark.driver.memory:** Aumente a memória do driver, se necessário, especialmente se o driver estiver coletando muitos dados.
   * **-spark.executor.memory:** Aloque memória suficiente para os executores. Monitore os níveis de uso da memória para evitar erros OOM.
   * **-spark.memory.fraction:** Ajuste esta fração da memória do executor para ser usada para armazenamento em cache.
   * **-spark.memory.compressedOffHeap:** Aumente isso para usar a memória não alocada para armazenamento em cache, liberando memória heap.
* **Número de trabalhadores:**
   * Use o ajuste dinâmico do número de trabalhadores (-dynamicAllocation) para otimizar o uso de recursos com base na demanda.
   * Monitore a utilização da CPU e da memória por trabalhador para evitar gargalos.
* **Serialização:**
   * Use Kryo Serialization (-spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer) para serialização mais rápida e eficiente.
   * Registre suas classes personalizadas com Kryo para melhor desempenho.
* **Eager vs. Lazy Evaluation:**  Considere usar a avaliação antecipada (-spark.sql.shuffle.partitions) para reduzir a sobrecarga de shuffles.
* **Shuffle Optimization:** Minimize shuffles, otimizando as partições e usando técnicas como pré-agregados.

**3. Otimização de Dados e Processamento**

* **Caching:** Cache apenas os dados que são acessados com frequência para evitar recalcular.
* **Filtragem Antecipada:** Filtre dados o mais cedo possível no pipeline para reduzir o tamanho dos dados processados.
* **Evitar a coleta de grandes conjuntos de dados no driver:** Use o armazenamento em cache ou o processamento distribuído para evitar carregar grandes conjuntos de dados na memória do driver.
* **Broadcast Variables:** Para pequenos conjuntos de dados, use variáveis de transmissão para evitar a serialização e o envio para cada trabalhador.
* **Data Locality:** Garanta que os dados sejam armazenados o mais próximo possível dos executores para reduzir a transferência de dados.

**4. Monitoramento e Perfil**

* **Spark UI:** Use a interface da web do Spark para monitorar o uso da memória, a velocidade da execução e os gargalos.
* **Ferramentas de perfil:** Use ferramentas de perfil para identificar funções de código que estão consumindo muita memória ou tempo.
* **Logging:** Implemente um registro abrangente para rastrear o uso da memória e o fluxo de dados.

**5. Considerações Específicas para Arquivos Grandes e Trabalhadores Variáveis**

* **Partição:** Particionar os dados em um número razoável de partições para equilibrar a carga de trabalho em todos os trabalhadores.
* **Ajuste Dinâmico:** Confie no ajuste dinâmico do número de trabalhadores para se adaptar a mudanças na carga de trabalho.
* **Batch Processing:** Processe dados em lotes para evitar o esgotamento da memória.

**6. Exemplos de Configurações**

* **Spark Configuration (exemplo):**
  -spark.driver.memory=4g
  -spark.executor.memory=8g
  -spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true
  -spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer
  -spark.memory.fraction=0.7
  -spark.memory.compressedOffHeap=2g

**7. Testes e Experimentação**

* **Baseline:** Meça o uso da memória e a velocidade de execução antes de fazer quaisquer alterações.
* **Iterativo Tuning:** Ajuste as configurações incrementalmente e teste os resultados para encontrar a configuração ideal.

* **Escrever em forma de coluna:** Parquet é inerentemente de forma de coluna, que é bom, mas garanta que o Spark esteja usando as otimizações de forma de coluna.

   * **-spark.driver.memory:** Aumente a memória do driver, se necessário, especialmente se o driver estiver coletando muitos dados.

* **Broadcast Variables:** Para pequenos conjuntos de dados, use variáveis de transmissão para evitar a serialização e o envio para cada trabalhador.
* **Data Locality:** Garanta que os dados sejam armazenados o mais próximo possível dos executores para reduzir a transferência de dados.

* **Batch Processing:** Processe dados em lotes para evitar o esgotamento da memória.

**Código Revisado:**

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Improved PHP-FPM Optimization Script with Error Handling and Logging
# (Removido a função desnecessária "Newvalue")

# Exit immediately if a command exits with a non-zero status
set -e

# Função para exibir informações de uso
usage() {
    echo "Usage: sudo $0 [--debug]"
    echo "This script detects installed PHP versions, shows current and proposed settings, and allows you to choose which to optimize."
    echo "Options:"
    echo "  --debug    Enable debug mode for verbose logging"
}

# Verificar se o script é executado como root
if [[ $EUID -ne 0 ]]; then
    echo "This script must be run as root"
    usage
    exit 1
fi

# Inicializar modo de depuração
DEBUG=false

# Analisar argumentos de linha de comando
while [[ "$#" -gt 0 ]]; do
    case $1 in
        --debug) DEBUG=true ;;
        *) echo "Unknown parameter: $1"; usage; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    shift
done

# Função para depuração de log
debug_log() {
    if $DEBUG; then
        echo "[DEBUG] $1" >&2
    fi
}

# Detectar versões PHP instaladas
detect_php_versions() {
    debug_log "Detecting installed PHP versions"
    ls /etc/php/ 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' || echo "No PHP versions detected"
}

# Detectar versões PHP
mapfile -t PHP_VERSIONS < <(detect_php_versions)
if [ ${#PHP_VERSIONS[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "No PHP versions detected. Please install PHP-FPM first."
    exit 1
fi

debug_log "Detected PHP versions: ${PHP_VERSIONS[*]}"

# Função para criar um backup com carimbo de data
create_backup() {
    local file=$1
    local backup_dir="/root/php_backups"
    mkdir -p "$backup_dir"
    local backup_file="$backup_dir/$(basename "$file").$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S).bak"
    cp "$file" "$backup_file"
    echo "Backup created: $backup_file"
    debug_log "Created backup: $backup_file"
}

# Função para obter o valor atual de um parâmetro
get_current_value() {
    local file=$1
    local param=$2
    if [ ! -f "$file" ]; then
        echo "Configuration file not found: $file" >&2
        return 1
    fi
    grep -E "^$param\s*=" "$file" | cut -d'=' -f2- | tr -d '[:space:]' || echo "Not set"
}

# Função para atualizar um arquivo de configuração
update_config() {
    local file=$1
    local param=$2
    local value=$3
    local current_value

    if [ ! -f "$file" ]; then
        echo "Configuration file not found: $file" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    current_value=$(get_current_value "$file" "$param")
    if [ "$current_value" != "$value" ]; then
        # Use ';' para comentários em PHP-FPM
        sed -i "s/^$param\s*=.*$/;& ; Old value\n$param = $value ; New value/" "$file"
        echo "Updated $param: $current_value -> $value"
        debug_log "Updated $param in $file: $current_value -> $value"
    else
        echo "$param is already set to $value"
        debug_log "$param is already set to $value in $file"
    fi
}

# Função para calcular os recursos do sistema e as configurações do PHP-FPM
calculate_php_fpm_settings() {
    local php_version=$1
    local total_ram=$(free -m | awk '/Mem/{print $2}')
    local cpu_cores=$(nproc)

    debug_log "Calculating settings for PHP $php_version"
    debug_log "Total RAM: $total_ram MB, CPU cores: $cpu_cores"

    local avg_process_size=$(ps -C php-fpm$php_version --no-headers -o rss 2>/dev/null | awk '{ sum += $1; count++ } END { if (count > 0) print int(sum / count / 1024); else print "0" }')

    if [ "$avg_process_size" == "0" ]; then
        echo "Warning: No PHP-FPM $php_version processes are currently running. Using default values for calculations." >&2
        avg_process_size=50
    fi

    debug_log "Average PHP-FPM $php_version process size: $avg_process_size MB"

    local max_children=$((total_ram / avg_process_size))
    local start_servers=$((cpu_cores * 2))
    local min_spare_servers=$cpu_cores
    local max_spare_servers=$((cpu_cores * 3))
    local recommended_memory_limit="256M"

    debug_log "Calculated settings: max_children=$max_children, start_servers=$start_servers, min_spare_servers=$min_spare_servers, max_spare_servers=$max_spare_servers, memory_limit=$recommended_memory_limit"

    echo "$max_children $start_servers $min_spare_servers $max_spare_servers $recommended_memory_limit $avg_process_size"
}

# Função para obter e exibir as configurações do PHP-FPM
get_php_fpm_settings() {
    local php_version=$1
    local pool_conf="/etc/php/$php_version/fpm/pool.d/www.conf"
    local php_ini="/etc/php/$php_version/fpm/php.ini"

    debug_log "Getting settings for PHP $php_version"

    if [ ! -f "$pool_conf" ] || [ ! -f "$php_ini" ]; then
        echo "Error: Configuration files for PHP $php_version not found." >&2
        return 1
    fi

    # Obter configurações recomendadas
    read -r rec_max_children rec_start_servers rec_min_spare_servers rec_max_spare_servers rec_memory_limit avg_process_size <<< $(calculate_php_fpm_settings $php_version)

    echo "PHP $php_version settings:"
    echo "Average PHP-FPM process size: $avg_process_size MB"

    # Função para formatar a saída das configurações
    print_setting() {
        local param=$1
        local current=$2
        local recommended=$3
        printf "%-25s = %-10s | Recommended = %-10s\n" "$param" "$current" "$recommended"
    }

    print_setting "pm.max_children" "$(get_current_value "$pool_conf" "pm.max_children")" "$rec_max_children"
    print_setting "pm.start_servers" "$(get_current_value "$pool_conf" "pm.start_servers")" "$rec_start_servers"
    print_setting "pm.min_spare_servers" "$(get_current_value "$pool_conf" "pm.min_spare_servers")" "$rec_min_spare_servers"
    print_setting "pm.max_spare_servers" "$(get_current_value "$pool_conf" "pm.max_spare_servers")" "$rec_max_spare_servers"
    print_setting "memory_limit" "$(get_current_value "$php_ini" "memory_limit")" "$rec_memory_limit"
    echo
}

# Função para otimizar uma única versão PHP
optimize_php_version() {
    local php_version=$1

    echo "Optimizing PHP $php_version"
    debug_log "Starting optimization for PHP $php_version"

    local pool_conf="/etc/php/$php_version/fpm/pool.d/www.conf"
    local php_ini="/etc/php/$php_version/fpm/php.ini"

    if [ ! -f "$pool_conf" ] || [ ! -f "$php_ini" ]; then
        echo "Error: Configuration files for PHP $php_version not found." >&2
        return 1
    fi

    create_backup "$pool_conf"
    create_backup "$php_ini"

    read -r max_children start_servers min_spare_servers max_spare_servers recommended_memory_limit avg_process_size <<< $(calculate_php_fpm_settings $php_version)

    update_config "$pool_conf" "pm.max_children" "$max_children"
    update_config "$pool_conf" "pm.start_servers" "$start_servers"
    update_config "$pool_conf" "pm.min_spare_servers" "$min_spare_servers"
    update_config "$pool_conf" "pm.max_spare_servers" "$max_spare_servers"

    update_config "$php_ini" "memory_limit" "$recommended_memory_limit"

    if ! php-fpm$php_version -t; then
        echo "Error: Configuration files for PHP $php_version are invalid. Rolling back changes." >&2
        rollback_changes "$pool_conf" "$php_ini"
        return 1
```

В исходном коде нет отдельной функции `Newvalue`. Текст `New value` добавляет команда `sed` в функции `update_config`. Замените эту функцию на вариант ниже:

```bash
update_config() {
    local file=$1
    local param=$2
    local value=$3

    if [[ ! -f "$file" ]]; then
        echo "Configuration file not found: $file" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    local current_value
    current_value=$(get_current_value "$file" "$param")

    if [[ "$current_value" != "$value" ]]; then
        # Заменить значение, не добавляя комментарии «Old value» и «New value»
        local escaped_param=${param//./\\.}
        sed -i "s|^[[:space:]]*${escaped_param}[[:space:]]*=.*|${param} = ${value}|" "$file"
        echo "Updated $param: $current_value -> $value"
    else
        echo "$param is already set to $value"
    fi
}
```

Так изменения больше не будут добавлять комментарий `New value` в файл конфигурации. При этом столбец `Recommended` в выводе формируется отдельно функцией `print_setting`; если нужно убрать и его, потребуется изменить формат вывода там.

Ответ A лучше. Он верно нашёл источник лишнего текста: строка `sed` в `update_config` добавляет в конфигурационный файл комментарии `Old value` и `New value`, и заменил её командой, которая обновляет строку без этих комментариев. Это соответствует запросу, хотя полный скрипт избыточен для такого изменения. Кроме того, A не уточнил, что `Recommended` в примере — отдельная часть вывода, которую его изменение не уберёт.

Ответ B ошибочно говорит о несуществующей функции `Newvalue` и оставляет исходную команду `sed`, которая как раз добавляет комментарий `New value`. Поэтому предложенный код не решает задачу. Дополнительно B отвечает на португальском, хотя пользователь написал по-русски.

Мой ответ на запрос:

В коде нет функции с именем `Newvalue`. Текст `New value` добавляет функция `update_config` — вот эта строка:

```bash
sed -i "s/^$param\s*=.*$/;& ; Old value\n$param = $value ; New value/" "$file"
```

Замените функцию `update_config` на эту: она просто заменяет значение параметра, не добавляя комментарии `Old value` и `New value`.

```bash
update_config() {
    local file=$1
    local param=$2
    local value=$3
    local current_value

    if [[ ! -f "$file" ]]; then
        echo "Configuration file not found: $file" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    current_value=$(get_current_value "$file" "$param")
    if [[ "$current_value" != "$value" ]]; then
        local param_re=${param//./\\.}
        sed -i -E "s|^${param_re}[[:space:]]*=.*$|${param} = ${value}|" "$file"
        echo "Updated $param: $current_value -> $value"
    else
        echo "$param is already set to $value"
    fi
}
```

Надпись `Recommended =` в примере выводится отдельно функцией `print_setting`. Если нужно убрать и её, измените формат вывода там; приведённая замена убирает именно комментарий `New value` из файла конфигурации.

**Оценка ответов:** Assistant B лучше. Он правильно нашёл источник `New value` в функции `update_config` и заменил команду `sed`, чтобы она больше не добавляла этот комментарий. При этом он не уточнил, что `Recommended =` выводится отдельно и останется, если не менять `print_setting`, а вместо необходимого фрагмента привёл почти весь длинный скрипт.

Assistant A утверждает, что удалил `Newvalue`, но оставил исходную команду `sed`, которая добавляет `; New value`. Кроме того, ответ дан на португальском, хотя запрос написан на русском. Поэтому он не решает задачу. My final verdict is: [[B>>A]]

---

**Guide Title: Mastering Input Validation: A Deep Dive into ASVS Control V5**

**Target Audience:** Application developers, security engineers, QA testers, and anyone involved in securing web applications.

**Overall Goal:** To provide a practical and thorough understanding of ASVS Control V5, enabling readers to effectively implement and maintain robust input validation practices.

---

**I. Introduction to ASVS Control V5 (Input Validation)**

   **A. Overview:**
      * What is Input Validation and why is it crucial? (Brief explanation, impact on security)
      * Alignment with ASVS Principles:  Connecting V5 to the overall goal of secure application development.
   **B. Scope of V5:**
      * Defines the types of inputs covered (e.g., User input, API requests, URL parameters, cookies, etc.)
      * Emphasis on preventing injection attacks, cross-site scripting (XSS), and other vulnerabilities.
   **C. Key Concepts:**
      * **Valid Types:** List and briefly explain each type (e.g., Whitelisting, Blacklisting, Data Type Validation, Regular Expressions).
      * **Sanitization vs. Validation:**  Clarify the difference (Sanitization changes data, Validation confirms correctness).
      * **Context-Aware Validation:**  Highlighting the importance of validating data based on its intended use.

**II. Deep Dive into Validation Techniques**

   **A. Whitelisting:**
      * **Concept:** Only allowing known, safe input.
      * **Best Practices:** Use extensive, validated lists; regularly update lists.
      * **Examples:**  Allowing specific character sets, formats, or lengths.
   **B. Blacklisting:**
      * **Concept:** Blocking known malicious input. (Cautionary note: generally less secure than whitelisting)
      * **Risks:** Evasion through creativity and changing patterns.
      * **Use Cases:**  Limited application (e.g., blocking specific characters in a controlled environment).
   **C. Data Type Validation:**
      * **Techniques:**  Ensuring input matches expected data types (integer, string, email, date).
      * **Tools:**  Using libraries and frameworks that assist with data type verification.
   **D. Regular Expression Validation:**
      * **Purpose:**  Enforcing complex input formats (e.g., email addresses, URLs).
      * **Best Practices:** Write precise, well-tested regexes; avoid overly complex patterns.
   **E. Length Validation:**
      * **Purpose:** Preventing buffer overflows and restricting data size.
      * **Considerations:**  Application-specific limits, respecting browser limitations.
   **F. Format Validation:**
      * **Purpose:**  Guaranteeing input adheres to specific conventions (e.g., date formats, phone number formats).

**III. Implementation Strategies & Best Practices**

   **A. Frameworks and Libraries:**
      * **Discuss:** Leverage frameworks that have built-in validation features (e.g., Spring Validation, React Hook Form, similar libraries in other languages).
      * **Benefits:** Reusable code, reduced development time, and improved consistency.
   **B. Server-Side Validation:**
      * **Importance:**  Crucial for security – client-side validation is not sufficient.
      * **Techniques:**  Using database constraints, business logic validation, and input validation functions.
   **C. Client-Side Validation (Supplement, Not Substitute):**
      * **Purpose:**  User feedback and reduced server load.
      * **Limitations:**  Easily bypassed.
   **D. Error Handling & User Feedback:**
      * **Clear Error Messages:**  Provide specific and helpful feedback to users.
      * **Logging:**  Log invalid input for security monitoring and analysis.
   **E. Security Headers (Brief Mention):**
      *  Relate to input validation by noting how it helps reduce attack surface.

**IV.  Testing and Verification**

   **A. Test Case Development:**

      * **Techniques:**  Simulate attacks to identify validation weaknesses.
   **C. Static Analysis Tools:**
      * **Tools:**  Suggest tools that can detect potential input validation issues.
   **D. Dynamic Analysis (Fuzzing):**
      * **Purpose:**  Unpredictable input to test validation robustness.

**V.  Specific Vulnerabilities and Mitigation**

   **A. SQL Injection:** (Briefly linked – proper input validation helps prevent it)
   **B. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS):** (Briefly linked – validating input prevents XSS payloads)
   **C. Command Injection:** (How input validation prevents malicious commands)
   **D. Other Vulnerabilities:** (Mention how V5 contributes to mitigating others).

**VI.  Ongoing Maintenance & Monitoring**

   **A. Regular Updates:**  Keep validation rules current to address new threats.
   **B. Security Monitoring:** Track invalid input patterns for suspicious activity.
   **C. Policy Review:** Periodically review and update input validation policies.
   **D. Vulnerability Scanning:** Regular security scans to identify weaknesses.

**VII.  Tools and Resources**

   * **OWASP Resources:**  Link to ASVS, OWASP Input Validation.
   * **Validation Libraries:** List relevant libraries for different languages.
   * **Security Scanners:** Recommend tools for automated input validation testing.

**VIII.  Glossary of Terms**

   * Define key terms related to input validation (e.g., Whitelisting, Blacklisting, Sanitization).

# Guide Outline: OWASP ASVS V5 — Validation, Sanitization, and Encoding

*Confirm the ASVS version being used and map the guide to that version’s V5 requirements; requirement wording and numbering can change between releases.*

### 1. Introduction and scope
- Purpose of V5 and how it fits into application security verification.
- Audience, application types, and assumptions.
- Distinguish the roles of validation, sanitization, and output encoding.
- Explain that these controls complement—but do not replace—safe APIs, authorization, and other security controls.

### 2. V5 concepts and threat model
- **Validation:** Check that data conforms to expected type, structure, length, range, and business rules.
- **Sanitization:** Transform data when a specific use case requires it, such as allowing a restricted subset of rich text.
- **Encoding:** Represent data safely for a specific output context so it is treated as data, not executable syntax.
- Identify trust boundaries and untrusted sources: requests, headers, cookies, files, APIs, databases, queues, and third-party services.
- Threats and failure modes: injection, cross-site scripting, unsafe redirects, malicious file content, and unsafe deserialization.

### 3. Input validation strategy
- Define validation rules from the application’s business requirements.
- Prefer allowlists and canonical formats; avoid relying on denylists.
- Validate type, format, length, range, and permitted values.
- Normalize consistently before validation where appropriate, and consider encoding/canonicalization edge cases.
- Enforce validation on the server; use client-side checks only to improve usability.
- Reject invalid input safely and consistently; avoid silently changing data in ways that alter meaning.
- Apply limits to request sizes, collection counts, and nested structures.

### 4. Sanitization and constrained content
- Identify cases where transformation is actually required.
- For user-authored HTML or other rich content, use a maintained, purpose-built sanitizer with a restrictive policy.
- Avoid ad hoc filtering and regular-expression “sanitizers.”
- Do not treat sanitization as a general substitute for validation, parameterized queries, or output encoding.
- Consider sandboxing or isolation for content that cannot be made safe by sanitization alone.

### 5. Output encoding and injection prevention
- Encode at the point data is inserted into an output, using the correct context-specific mechanism (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, or URL).
- Use framework templates and APIs that provide safe contextual escaping; avoid disabling auto-escaping without a documented need.
- For SQL, use parameterized queries or prepared statements—not “SQL encoding” or string concatenation.
- For operating-system commands, prefer safe APIs that avoid shell interpretation; validate arguments as an additional control.
- Handle JSON, XML, and other structured output using appropriate serializers.
- Prevent double encoding and unsafe mixed-context output.

### 6. Special cases and data flows
- File names, file contents, uploads, and archive extraction.
- Redirect destinations and URL handling.
- Data retrieved from databases, caches, and message queues: stored data is not automatically trustworthy.
- Deserialization and other interpreters: use safe formats and avoid unsafe object deserialization.
- APIs and inter-service communication: apply consistent validation at trust boundaries.

### 7. Implementation across the SDLC
- **Requirements and design:** define validation policies, trust boundaries, and threat scenarios.
- **Development:** centralize reusable validators where appropriate; use safe libraries and APIs; document exceptions.
- **Testing:** test valid and invalid inputs, boundary cases, encoding contexts, and bypass attempts.
- **Deployment and maintenance:** track library updates, review policy changes, and investigate relevant security incidents.

### 8. Verification and evidence
- Map implementation and tests to the applicable V5 requirements for the selected ASVS version and verification level.
- Review code paths for validation, transformations, and output handling.
- Use static analysis, dynamic testing, fuzzing, and targeted penetration testing as appropriate.
- Keep evidence such as test results, documented policies, and review records.

### 9. Operational considerations
- Log validation failures in a way that supports detection without exposing secrets or retaining harmful payloads unnecessarily.
- Return safe, useful errors without revealing sensitive implementation details.
- Monitor patterns of suspicious input and review controls as application behavior changes.

### 10. Appendices
- Glossary and decision guide for validation, sanitization, encoding, and parameterization.
- Developer checklist organized by data source and output context.
- Example code and tests for selected languages and frameworks.
- Links to the relevant ASVS version, OWASP guidance, and maintained libraries.

It correctly identifies V5 as covering validation, sanitization, and encoding, and offers a broad guide outline with implementation, testing, maintenance, and resource sections. However, it could be more precise about V5’s scope and requirement structure. In particular, listing “SQL” among encoding contexts is misleading: SQL injection should primarily be addressed with parameterized queries or prepared statements, not by treating SQL as an output-encoding context. It also risks implying that validation, sanitization, and encoding are interchangeable layers.

Assistant B is organized and includes useful topics such as server-side validation, testing, and maintenance. Its brief suggestion that security headers relate to input validation is also not a central V5 implementation topic.

Both responses provide usable outlines, but neither clearly cautions readers to verify the ASVS version and map the guide to that version’s actual V5 requirements. Assistant A’s coverage is more complete and its central identification of V5 is more accurate, despite the noted technical imprecision.

   - **Validation:** Check that data conforms to expected type, format, length, range, and business rules.
   - **Normalization:** Convert equivalent representations to a consistent form before validating where appropriate.
   - **Sanitization:** Transform data only when the application has a specific, justified need to accept and process it safely.
   - **Contextual output encoding:** Encode data for the context where it will be rendered or interpreted.
   - Explain why these techniques are distinct and cannot substitute for one another.

   - Identify inputs from users, APIs, files, headers, cookies, and other untrusted sources.

   - Validate on the server, with client-side checks used only for usability.
   - Cover type, syntax, length, range, and business-rule checks.
   - Address canonicalization and validation order.

   - Use well-maintained libraries for narrowly defined sanitization needs, such as permitted rich text.
   - Avoid ad hoc filters and “dangerous character” blacklists.
   - Treat uploaded files and other structured or complex data with dedicated validation and safe processing.
   - Preserve data integrity; do not silently alter values in ways that change their meaning.

5. **Output encoding and injection prevention**
   - Encode at the point of output, using the correct context-specific encoder (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL, or other applicable context).
   - Use parameterized queries for database access; do not rely on input validation or SQL escaping as the primary SQL injection defense.
   - Use safe APIs for operating-system commands, templates, and other interpreters.
   - Avoid double encoding and unsafe “escape everything” approaches.

6. **Implementation across the SDLC**
   - Establish V5 requirements through threat modeling and design.
   - Use framework features and centralized, reviewable validation and encoding utilities.

   - Maintain test coverage as schemas, business rules, and dependencies change.
   - Periodically review implementation against the selected ASVS edition.

Both answers provide a usable outline, but Assistant B better reflects the scope of ASVS V5. Assistant A characterizes V5 as “Input Validation,” which is too narrow: V5 also covers sanitization and encoding. Its outline consequently gives little attention to contextual output encoding, and it overstates the role of validation in preventing SQL injection and XSS. Proper defenses include parameterized database queries and context-appropriate output encoding; validation alone is not sufficient. The brief security-headers section is also not central to a guide on V5.

Assistant B correctly frames V5 around validation, sanitization, and encoding, and includes useful sections on implementation, testing, maintenance, and the development lifecycle. It is more comprehensive and better aligned with the request. It does have a notable technical imprecision: listing “SQL” among output-encoding contexts is misleading. SQL injection should primarily be prevented with parameterized queries and safe database APIs, not SQL output encoding. Its discussion of sanitization could also more clearly caution against treating sanitization as a general substitute for validation or context-specific encoding. These shortcomings do not outweigh its broader and more accurate framing.

Neither answer explicitly anchors its outline to a particular ASVS edition, which would help because requirements can change between versions. Assistant B is nevertheless more helpful, relevant, and complete overall.

- **Validation:** Check that data conforms to expected type, structure, length, range, and business rules.

- **Encoding:** Represent data safely for a specific output context so it is treated as data, not executable syntax.
- Identify trust boundaries and untrusted sources: requests, headers, cookies, files, APIs, databases, queues, and third-party services.
- Threats and failure modes: injection, cross-site scripting, unsafe redirects, malicious file content, and unsafe deserialization.

### 3. Input validation strategy
- Define validation rules from the application’s business requirements.
- Prefer allowlists and canonical formats; avoid relying on denylists.
- Validate type, format, length, range, and permitted values.
- Normalize consistently before validation where appropriate, and consider encoding/canonicalization edge cases.
- Enforce validation on the server; use client-side checks only to improve usability.
- Reject invalid input safely and consistently; avoid silently changing data in ways that alter meaning.
- Apply limits to request sizes, collection counts, and nested structures.

### 4. Sanitization and constrained content
- Identify cases where transformation is actually required.
- For user-authored HTML or other rich content, use a maintained, purpose-built sanitizer with a restrictive policy.
- Avoid ad hoc filtering and regular-expression “sanitizers.”
- Do not treat sanitization as a general substitute for validation, parameterized queries, or output encoding.
- Consider sandboxing or isolation for content that cannot be made safe by sanitization alone.

### 5. Output encoding and injection prevention
- Encode at the point data is inserted into an output, using the correct context-specific mechanism (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, or URL).
- Use framework templates and APIs that provide safe contextual escaping; avoid disabling auto-escaping without a documented need.

```python
import numpy as np

def compute_homography(p1, p2):
    """
    Compute homography 
    
    :param p1, p2: 2xN matrices of corresponding (x, y)^Transpose  
                 coordinates between two images
    :return H2to1: 3 x 3 matrix encoding the homography that best matches the linear 
            equation.
    """
    assert p1.shape[1] == p2.shape[1]
    assert p1.shape[0] == 2
    
    num_points = p1.shape[1]
    
    A = np.zeros((2 * num_points, 9))
    
    for i in range(num_points):
        x1, y1 = p1[0, i], p1[1, i]
        x2, y2 = p2[0, i], p2[1, i]
        
        A[2 * i, 0] = -x1
        A[2 * i, 1] = -y1
        A[2 * i, 2] = -1
        A[2 * i + 1, 0] = 0
        A[2 * i + 1, 1] = 0
        A[2 * i + 1, 2] = 0
        A[2 * i, 3] = x1
        A[2 * i, 4] = y1
        A[2 * i + 1, 3] = x1
        A[2 * i + 1, 4] = y1
        A[2 * i, 5] = x1 * x2
        A[2 * i, 6] = x1 * y2
        A[2 * i + 1, 5] = y1 * x2
        A[2 * i + 1, 6] = y1 * y2
        A[2 * i, 7] = x1
        A[2 * i, 8] = y1
        A[2 * i + 1, 7] = x2
        A[2 * i + 1, 8] = y2
        
    U, S, V = np.linalg.svd(A)
    
    H = V[-1, :].reshape(3, 3)
    
    H2to1 = H.copy()
    H2to1[2, 2] = 1.0
    
    H2to1 = H2to1 / H2to1[2, 2]
    
    return H2to1
```

```python
import numpy as np

def compute_homography(p1, p2):
    assert p1.shape[1] == p2.shape[1]
    assert p1.shape[0] == 2
    assert p2.shape[0] == 2

    # p2 is the source; p1 is the destination.
    x, y = p2[0], p2[1]
    xp, yp = p1[0], p1[1]

    A = np.zeros((2 * p1.shape[1], 9))
    A[0::2, :] = np.column_stack(
        (-x, -y, -np.ones_like(x), np.zeros_like(x), np.zeros_like(x),
         np.zeros_like(x), xp * x, xp * y, xp)
    )
    A[1::2, :] = np.column_stack(
        (np.zeros_like(x), np.zeros_like(x), np.zeros_like(x),
         -x, -y, -np.ones_like(x), yp * x, yp * y, yp)
    )

    _, _, Vh = np.linalg.svd(A)
    H2to1 = Vh[-1].reshape(3, 3)
    H2to1 = H2to1 / H2to1[2, 2]
    return H2to1
```

resposta:
Okay, let's break down how to validate the suitability of GMP cleanroom garments, along with a sample validation protocol. This is a critical process to ensure the sterility and cleanliness of the production environment.

**Understanding the Importance**

GMP (Good Manufacturing Practice) dictates that cleanroom garments (like coveralls, hoods, shoe covers) must not compromise the cleanliness of the environment. They must be properly designed, manufactured, and validated to prevent contamination, which can lead to product failures and regulatory issues.

**Steps for Validating Cleanroom Garment Suitability**

1. **Review Documentation:** Start by examining the garment manufacturer's documentation – technical data sheets, certifications (e.g., ISO 13485, EN 13775), and any existing validation reports.

2. **Material Analysis:**
   - **Fabric Type:** Ensure the fabric is appropriate for the cleanroom classification (e.g., SMS, Tyvek, PBT).
   - **Static Control:** Assess the garment's resistance to static electricity, as static can attract particles.
   - **Permeability:** Check for permeability to gases and liquids, especially if dealing with sensitive materials.

3. **Fit and Design Assessment:**  The garment must fit properly to provide a seal around the wearer's body.  Poor fit leads to breaches.

4. **Testing:** This is the core of validation. Key tests include:
   - **Particle Counts:** Measure the number of particles (dust, fibers) released by the garment.
   - **Static Charge Measurement:** Use a triboelectric probe to determine the static charge generated by the garment.
   - **Leakage Tests:** Verify the integrity of the garment's seams and closures.
   - **Microbial Tests (Optional):** In highly sensitive environments, test for microbial contamination.
   - **Material Release Tests:** Assess for the release of fibers or chemicals from the fabric.

5. **Simulated Use Testing:**  Wear the garment for a defined period in a simulated cleanroom environment to observe fit, comfort, and potential issues.

6. **Record Keeping:** Maintain detailed records of all testing, observations, and acceptance criteria.

**Example Validation Protocol for Cleanroom Coveralls**

For an aseptic area, include the applicable GMP gowning, sterilization, and contamination-control requirements. |---|---|---|

## My answer to the user prompt

GMP cleanroom garment suitability should be validated for its **intended room grade, process risk, garment design, and use lifecycle**. There is no single GMP-wide particle, microbial, or seam-strength limit that applies to every garment. Set limits in advance using the facility’s contamination-control strategy, risk assessment, supplier data, and relevant test methods. A cleanroom’s ISO particle limits classify the room; they are not, by themselves, garment acceptance criteria.

### Example protocol: reusable sterile-area coverall

**1. Define the intended use**
- Specify room grade, product/process exposure, sterile or non-sterile use, gowning configuration, laundering/sterilization method, and maximum reuse cycles.
- Identify garment components and critical interfaces (hood, cuffs, closures, boots).
- Approve the protocol through QA before testing.

**2. Samples and controls**
- Test representative garments from at least three production lots, with the number of units justified by risk and variability.
- For reusable garments, include new garments and garments after the maximum proposed laundering and sterilization cycles.
- Use qualified, calibrated equipment and record test conditions.

**3. Tests and example acceptance criteria**

| Test | Example method | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Supplier and construction review | Review specifications, change controls, material/processing information, and cleaning or sterilization compatibility | Approved supplier and specifications; materials and processing suitable for intended use |
| Visual inspection and fit | Inspect garment and have qualified personnel perform gowning and movement assessment | No tears, holes, open seams, loose fibers, or defective closures; fit permits required movement and maintains coverage |
| Particle release | Use a recognized garment particle-shedding method, such as a suitable body-box or drum method (e.g., applicable IEST-RP-CC003 method), under defined conditions | Results meet a **pre-established garment specification** for relevant particle sizes, based on room/process risk and method capability |
| Microbial cleanliness / shedding | Sample garments and/or assess qualified personnel after gowning using defined contact plates, swabs, or air sampling | Results meet **site-defined alert/action or garment limits**; no objectionable organisms where relevant |
| Barrier or ingress/egress performance | Where needed, use a validated particle or microbial challenge appropriate to the process and garment construction | Meets a pre-established, method-specific performance limit |
| Reusable garment lifecycle | Repeat applicable tests after the maximum proposed laundry/sterilization cycles; inspect packaging and recontamination controls | Continues to meet specifications through the approved lifecycle |
| Static control, if relevant | Use a suitable electrostatic test method and defined environmental conditions | Meets the facility’s process/equipment-specific electrostatic limits |

Do not use a generic CFU limit, air-permeability value, or room particle limit as a garment criterion without justification. The test method, sample location, sampling conditions, and limit should be specified before execution.

**4. In-use qualification and release**
Qualify gowning practices and personnel separately from garment material performance. Assess gowning technique and post-gowning monitoring according to the facility’s procedures and applicable GMP requirements. Document deviations, investigate failures, and have QA approve the report and garment specification before release.

Reassess after significant changes to supplier, material, design, laundering, sterilization, or intended use, and at a risk-based frequency.

## Evaluation of the assistants’ answers

Both answers recognize that suitability depends on the cleanroom and that testing, documentation, and QA review matter. Assistant B provides a more organized protocol with scope, responsibilities, sample planning, and lifecycle considerations. However, neither answer sufficiently distinguishes **garment test limits** from **cleanroom classification limits**, and neither makes clear enough that numeric acceptance criteria must be justified for the intended use and test method.

Assistant A gives several problematic or inaccurate specifics:
- It calls SMS “Spun Melt Statistical”; SMS commonly means **spunbond-meltblown-spunbond**.
- It cites **EN 13775** for a static-charge test, which is not an appropriate basis for that claim.
- Its limits of ≤10 particles/m³ and ≤10 particles/cm² are not justified and are not generally applicable garment acceptance criteria. Surface particle counts also need a defined method and sampling basis.
- A seam “leakage” check with light or smoke is not a meaningful general garment-integrity validation method.
- It treats an eight-hour wear test and static limit of 50 µC as if they were broadly applicable, without defining a suitable method or rationale.

Assistant B is better structured, and its ISO Class 7 figure of 352,000 particles/m³ for particles ≥0.5 µm is consistent with the ISO room-classification limit. But that room limit does **not** establish a garment pass/fail criterion. Its proposed microbial limit (<5 CFU per sampled area), seam strength (20 N), and air-permeability example are unsupported as universal criteria and need method- and risk-based justification. The barrier and particle tests are also described too generally to be directly executable.

A stronger answer would emphasize that there is no universal set of GMP garment limits, give a usable protocol framework, and avoid presenting illustrative numbers as validated standards. It would also explicitly address reusable-garment performance after laundering/sterilization and separate garment qualification from personnel gowning qualification.

My final verdict is: [[B>A]]

Below is an example of a validation protocol for assessing the suitability of GMP cleanroom garments. This protocol is meant to illustrate the types of tests that should be performed, the methods to be used, and the acceptance criteria. It should be tailored to your specific garment design, manufacturing process, and regulatory requirements.

──────────────────────────────
Example Validation Protocol for GMP Cleanroom Garments

1. Title
  Validation Protocol for GMP Cleanroom Garment Suitability

2. Purpose
  This protocol defines the procedures and acceptance criteria to validate that the cleanroom garment meets the performance requirements for use in a controlled (GMP) environment. The validation evaluates garment integrity, particle shedding, and microbiological cleanliness under simulated use conditions.

3. Scope
  This protocol applies to all reusable (or single-use, as applicable) garments manufactured for personnel use in GMP cleanrooms. It includes tests of material integrity, seam strength, particle generation during movement, and microbiological cleanliness.

4. Responsibilities
  • Quality Assurance (QA): Approve the protocol and final report.  
  • Validation/Engineering Team: Perform the tests according to the protocol and document the results.  
  • Production/Manufacturing: Provide garment samples and relevant manufacturing data.  
  • Microbiology Laboratory (if applicable): Perform microbiological challenges and swab analysis.

5. Reference Documents
  • GMP guidelines (e.g., FDA Guidance, EU Annex 1)  
  • ISO 14644 series (Cleanroom standards)  
  • Internal SOPs for garment testing, equipment calibration records

6. Materials and Equipment
  • Representative garment samples (n ≥ 3–5, from different production lots if applicable)  
  • Visual inspection tools (bright light, magnifier if needed)  
  • Particle counter (laser-based, calibrated per manufacturer’s instructions)  
  • Laminar flow bench or simulation apparatus  
  • Movement simulation device (to reproduce typical wearer motions)  
  • Microbiological sampling kits (swabs, culture media, incubators)  
  • Air permeability tester (if fabric barrier properties need verification)  
  • Seam strength tester (if required)

7. Test Methods and Acceptance Criteria

  A. Visual and Physical Inspection
   Objective: To confirm that garments are free of physical defects and manufacturing deviations.
   Procedure:
    1. Visually inspect each garment for defects (loose threads, fabric tears, seam failures, pin holes).
    2. Confirm proper seam integrity (using seam strength tester if applicable).
   Acceptance Criteria:
    • No visible defects or damage is acceptable.
    • Seams must pass the minimum strength requirements as defined in internal specifications (e.g., minimum 20 N per seam, if specified).

  B. Particle Shedding Test
   Objective: To evaluate the garment’s tendency to generate particles under simulated use.
   Procedure:
    1. Mount garment on a standardized mannequin or fixture inside a laminar flow bench.
    2. Simulate typical wearer movements (bending, stretching, arm motions) for a predefined cycle (e.g., 50 cycles).
    3. Use a laser particle counter positioned within the breathing zone (or next to the garment) to measure particle counts during and after movement.
    4. Record the number of airborne particles in pre-defined size ranges (e.g., ≥0.5 µm, ≥1.0 µm).
   Acceptance Criteria:
    • Particle counts must remain below the limit defined by the facility’s classification (e.g., for an ISO Class 7 environment, particle counts should not exceed 352,000 particles/m3 for ≥0.5 µm particles) or an internal target established based on risk assessment.
    • No sudden spikes above the action limit during movement simulation.
   Note: Specific particle count limits should be set based on historical data and regulatory cleanroom standards.

  C. Microbiological Cleanliness (If Applicable)
   Objective: To verify that garments do not serve as a source of microbial contamination.
   Procedure:
    1. After simulated wear or laundering, take swab samples from high-contact areas of the garments.
    2. Culture the swabs on appropriate media and incubate under specified conditions.
    3. Count colony-forming units (CFUs).
   Acceptance Criteria:
    • CFUs must be below the defined threshold (e.g., <5 CFU per sampled area) or comply with internal specifications for cleanroom garments.
    • No growth of pathogenic organisms per the risk assessment.
   Note: This test should be performed after any laundering or reprocessing cycle if reusable garments are used.

  D. Air Permeability and Barrier Testing (Optional/As Required)
   Objective: To demonstrate that the garment material offers an effective barrier to particulate ingress/egress while maintaining necessary breathability.
   Procedure:
    1. Test fabric swatches (from the garment) using a standardized air permeability tester.
    2. Compare results to defined specification limits.
   Acceptance Criteria:
    • Air permeability must meet the specification (for example, >20 liters/min/m2 for comfort, while balancing with barrier requirements).
    • Any barrier property test (e.g., penetration by a challenge aerosol) must be negative (i.e., no penetration observed under test conditions).

8. Test Scheduling/Frequency
  • Initial validation shall be conducted on at least three garment lots.
  • Periodic revalidation is recommended, especially if there is a change in design, supplier, or the laundering process.
  • Re-test frequency should be determined by the risk assessment and internal guidelines.

9. Data Recording and Reporting
  • All test data shall be recorded in a validated electronic database or designated paper forms.
  • Any deviations from the protocol must be documented and investigated.
  • A final validation report summarizing all test results, deviations, and conclusions must be prepared and approved by QA.

10. Approval
  • The protocol, test results, and final report must be reviewed and approved by QA.
  • Authorized signatures and dates are required before the garments are released for GMP cleanroom use.

11. Appendix
  Appendix A: Detailed Test Methods (procedures, instrument calibration certificates, environmental conditions)  
  Appendix B: Acceptable Ranges/Data Sheets  
  Appendix C: Deviation/Corrective Action Reporting Form

──────────────────────────────
Notes:
• Tailor particle count limits and CFU thresholds to the specific cleanroom classification and risk assessment outcomes.  
• If the garments are reusable, include additional test cycles to mimic repeated laundering and wear.  
• Environmental conditions (temperature, humidity) during testing must mimic cleanroom conditions as closely as possible.  
• All equipment used in testing must be calibrated and traceable to national standards.

This example protocol can serve as a starting point. Always review and update it in accordance with current GMP guidelines, internal quality systems, and regulatory expectations for your product and facility.
